commit_message:
[Vulkan] HAL Rewrite (#24459)

This should be compatible with old VMFBs. I expect some platforms to
possibly need feature backfill or compatibility support but our testing
story is too thin to know yet. The big shift here is baselining on
Vulkan 1.3. With a bit of extra work we could stretch back to 1.2 with
extensions.

---

This PR replaces the legacy Vulkan HAL with a new implementation built
around the current HAL queue contract, native Vulkan command recording,
explicit feature negotiation, buffer-device-address dispatch, direct
transfer/file paths, and HAL-native profiling.

The old driver worked (and was some of the oldest IREE code, written
before it was even open sourced!), but it grew around synchronous
submission, descriptor-set dispatch, and direct recording assumptions
that do not map well to modern IREE workloads. In particular, it did not
give us a clean way to model asynchronous queue frontiers, reusable
command-buffer replay, file/transfer operations, BDA dispatch, or
backend-visible profiling statistics without continuing to layer
compatibility paths on top of the old design.

The new driver has two goals:

- Keep descriptor ABI compatibility for existing Vulkan executables.
- Make the optimized Vulkan path descriptor-free, replayable,
observable, and aligned with the same command-buffer model used by newer
HAL backends.

## Driver Architecture

The implementation is organized around explicit ownership boundaries:

- `api.*` defines Vulkan HAL feature policy, extension names, and public
option translation.
- `physical_device.*` owns enumeration, device snapshots, baseline
validation, extension discovery, feature/property capture, and
queue-family description.
- `logical_device.*` owns logical-device creation, queue selection,
topology, allocator installation, executable-cache creation, file
import, and device queries.
- `queue.*` owns queue submission, timeline epochs, dependency
resolution, native command-buffer allocation, asynchronous completion,
staging, direct dispatch, transfer/file operation recording, profiling
timestamps, and replay cache statistics.
- `command_buffer.*` owns reusable HAL command-buffer storage, compact
command records, descriptor/BDA requirement accounting, resource
lifetime tracking, and native replay into `VkCommandBuffer`.
- `executable.*` owns Vulkan executable loading, SPIR-V module/pipeline
creation, descriptor ABI metadata, BDA ABI metadata, raw BDA executable
support, global lookup, and per-pipeline dispatch metadata.

Unsupported cases are rejected at the boundary where they are
discovered. The rewrite intentionally avoids silent fallbacks that would
hide missing Vulkan features or route hot paths through emulation.

## Queue Model

The new queue implementation uses Vulkan timeline semaphores as queue
epochs. Each selected queue lane tracks accepted submissions,
signal/wait frontiers, completion state, and pending cleanup. HAL
semaphore dependencies are resolved through the queue path without
assuming FIFO submission order.

Queue submission supports:

- execution barriers;
- queue allocation and deallocation;
- sparse binding;
- fill, update, copy, read, and write operations;
- direct dispatch;
- reusable command-buffer execute;
- file-backed staging;
- host callbacks.

This replaces the old split between synchronous direct operations and
special driver-side helper paths. Queue work now enters through one
scheduling model and retires through one completion model.

## Executable And Dispatch ABIs

The driver supports both Vulkan executable ABIs:

- `vulkan-spirv-fb`, the descriptor ABI, for compatibility with existing
descriptor-set storage-buffer executables.
- `vulkan-spirv-bda-v1` and `vulkan-spirv-bda-raw`, the BDA ABIs, for
descriptor-free dispatch through a device-address binding table.

The descriptor ABI now uses `VK_KHR_push_descriptor` when the device
supports it and the pipeline layout fits the extension limits. That
removes descriptor pool allocation and descriptor-set update overhead
from the descriptor compatibility path.

BDA is the primary performance path. The runtime publishes a compact
device-address binding table and the shader reads resource addresses
directly. Reusable command buffers can keep the native Vulkan command
body resident while only the published BDA table bytes change between
executions.

## Device Compatibility

This rewrite intentionally raises the Vulkan baseline. The
driver-created instance requests Vulkan 1.3 by default, and
physical-device enumeration only accepts devices with:

- `apiVersion >= VK_API_VERSION_1_3`;
- `timelineSemaphore`;
- `scalarBlockLayout`;
- `synchronization2`;
- at least one compute-capable queue family.

That baseline is what lets the queue use timeline-semaphore epochs,
express barriers through synchronization2, and keep shader/storage
layouts consistent without carrying old synchronization and layout
compatibility paths. The target is Vulkan 1.3, not Vulkan 1.4; Vulkan
1.3 has been the stable modern Vulkan baseline since [January
2022](https://docs.vulkan.org/guide/latest/versions.html#vulkan-13-features-breakdown).

`bufferDeviceAddress` is a second gate for the optimized BDA dispatch
ABI. A device can still use descriptor-ABI executables without BDA, but
`vulkan-spirv-bda-v1` and `vulkan-spirv-bda-raw` require BDA because
their binding table is a table of device addresses instead of descriptor
bindings.

Optional capabilities remain opportunistic:

- `VK_KHR_push_descriptor` accelerates the descriptor compatibility path
when available.
- `VK_EXT_calibrated_timestamps` improves profile clock correlation when
available.
- external memory, host memory import, sparse binding, and sparse
residency are enabled only when the device and requested HAL features
require them.

As a rough ecosystem sanity check, the [Vulkan Hardware Database
`apiVersion`
distribution](https://vulkan.gpuinfo.org/displaycoreproperty.php?name=apiversion)
reports Vulkan 1.3 or 1.4 in 24,376 of 44,893 submitted all-platform
reports (54.3%). The desktop slice is stronger: 12,446 of 19,758
[Windows
reports](https://vulkan.gpuinfo.org/displaycoreproperty.php?name=apiversion&platform=windows)
(63.0%) and 9,547 of 15,964 [Linux
reports](https://vulkan.gpuinfo.org/displaycoreproperty.php?name=apiversion&platform=linux)
(59.8%) are Vulkan 1.3+. Android is lower at 2,400 of 7,832 [Android
reports](https://vulkan.gpuinfo.org/displaycoreproperty.php?name=apiversion&platform=android)
(30.6%), which matches the fact that this rewrite is primarily aimed at
modern desktop/server Vulkan rather than old mobile Vulkan stacks.

The required feature bits are not the practical compatibility cliff
within the modern driver cohort: gpuinfo.org's all-platform [Vulkan 1.2
feature coverage](https://vulkan.gpuinfo.org/listfeaturescore12.php) and
[Vulkan 1.3 feature
coverage](https://vulkan.gpuinfo.org/listfeaturescore13.php) list
`timelineSemaphore` at 99.88%, `scalarBlockLayout` at 98.82%,
`synchronization2` at 99.82%, and `bufferDeviceAddress` at 98.47%. Treat
those numbers as [community-submitted device/report coverage rather than
market share](https://vulkan.gpuinfo.org/about.php), but they are useful
evidence that the meaningful bump is the Vulkan 1.3 driver baseline, not
an obscure optional-feature combination.

## Command Buffers

HAL command buffers record structured Vulkan command records instead of
trying to expose old direct-command-buffer behavior through the HAL API.
During recording the driver accumulates:

- descriptor requirements for descriptor ABI replay;
- BDA publication byte requirements for BDA replay;
- retained resources for safe command-buffer lifetime;
- dispatch metadata required for profiling and native replay.

At queue execution time the command buffer is replayed into a native
`VkCommandBuffer`. BDA command buffers can use the native replay cache:
the cache keeps reusable native command buffers and BDA publication
storage per queue lane, skips publication when binding slots are
unchanged, and exposes
hits, misses, forks, bypasses, trims, peak instance count, and peak
publication bytes through `query_i64` counters under
`vulkan.queue.native_replay_cache`.

Descriptor command buffers currently bypass native replay caching
because their replayed Vulkan commands embed binding-table-dependent
descriptor state. This matches the old indirect-command-buffer shape:
the old driver recorded deferred HAL commands for binding-table command
buffers and materialized a native Vulkan command buffer during each
`queue_execute`. The rewrite keeps that compatibility contract, uses
push descriptors when available, and reserves resident native replay for
BDA command buffers where the command body is independent of the
execute-time binding table.

## Transfer And File Paths

Queue transfers are native Vulkan operations in the new driver. Fill,
update, and copy are recorded directly into Vulkan command buffers.
Unaligned fill and update edges are patched with driver-owned built-in
pipelines instead of falling through an emulated transfer layer.

File reads and writes use storage-buffer-backed files directly when
available. Host-backed files are staged through device-visible memory
and the async file path, keeping file operations on the same
queue/completion model as the rest of the driver.

## Profiling And Statistics

Profiling is built into the queue and command-buffer paths. The driver
records HAL executable metadata, command-buffer metadata, queue events,
queue device timestamps, and optional per-dispatch timestamp ranges
through the local HAL profile recorder used by `iree-profile`.

Timestamp query pools are queue-owned and cached. Calibrated timestamp
support is used when available to relate Vulkan device ticks to the HAL
profile timeline, and invalid calibrated ranges are marked instead of
forcing a bad clock fit.

The driver also exposes backend statistics through device queries,
including native replay cache behavior, BDA publication cache behavior,
and timestamp query cache behavior. These counters make performance
paths inspectable instead of requiring driver-internal debugging.

## Performance Characterization

The performance goal of the rewrite is simple: Vulkan command buffers
should be cheap to submit because the backend records native Vulkan work
once and replays that work directly. The benchmark rows below keep that
contract visible by separating host submit cost from end-to-end drain
cost:

- Submit-only rows time command-buffer replay and queue submission, with
the final completion wait outside the timed region.
- Submit + wait rows include the final completion wait and therefore
include driver and device drain behavior.

All rows are release Google Benchmark medians. The benchmark set
compares the old descriptor-set Vulkan HAL, the new
descriptor-compatible Vulkan path, the new BDA Vulkan dispatch ABI, and
AMDGPU AQL/PM4 command-buffer replay. Those are distinct mechanisms, so
the tables keep them separate instead of turning the result into a
single backend ranking.

### Vulkan Command-Buffer Replay

Homogeneous 10K-dispatch command-buffer replay:

| Path | ABI | Submit-only | Submit + wait | Interpretation |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Old Vulkan HAL | Descriptor sets | 5.139 ms | 5.609 ms | Deferred HAL
command buffer replayed into Vulkan and bound descriptor sets for every
dispatch. |
| New Vulkan HAL | Push descriptors | 2.072 ms | 5.257 ms | Descriptor
compatibility path avoids descriptor pool/set churn and cuts host replay
cost by 2.48x. |
| New Vulkan HAL | BDA | 12.361 us | 1.435 ms | Native BDA replay hits
the native replay cache and cuts host replay cost by 416x vs old Vulkan.
|

The descriptor row is the compatibility story: the new HAL is still
faster than old Vulkan when running the legacy descriptor ABI. The BDA
row is the design story: when the compiler targets the new ABI, replay
becomes one cached native command-buffer submission instead of a
per-dispatch descriptor-binding loop.

For command-buffer recording, the hot unvalidated/unretained path
remains close to the old implementation, and the default checked path is
now within about 24 us over 5K dispatches:

| Path | Recording mode | 5K-dispatch record-only |
| --- | --- | ---: |
| Old Vulkan HAL | Default validation/retention | 183.547 us |
| Old Vulkan HAL | Unvalidated + unretained | 93.925 us |
| New Vulkan HAL | Default validation/retention | 207.266 us |
| New Vulkan HAL | Unvalidated, retained | 113.191 us |
| New Vulkan HAL | Validated, unretained | 190.903 us |
| New Vulkan HAL | Unvalidated + unretained | 97.998 us |

That distinction matters for interpreting the submit rows. The rewrite
is not winning by making unchecked recording magically cheaper; it is
winning because recorded BDA command buffers replay as native Vulkan
work instead of walking the IREE deferred command stream on every
submission. The record-only default delta is validation and retention
bookkeeping on a cold path; the repeated-use win is in the submit/replay
path.

### Direct Transfer Host Cost

Queue transfer operations now go through native queue paths instead of
the old host-side emulated command-buffer path. The strong claim here is
submit-only host overhead:

| Operation | Size | Old Vulkan submit-only | New Vulkan submit-only |
Speedup |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Copy batch x20 | 4 B | 304 us | 46 us | 6.54x |
| Copy batch x20 | 4 KiB | 309 us | 57 us | 5.47x |
| Fill batch x20 | 4 B | 295 us | 48 us | 6.09x |
| Fill batch x20 | 4 KiB | 285 us | 57 us | 5.02x |
| Update batch x20 | 4 B | 278 us | 59 us | 4.75x |
| Update batch x20 | 4 KiB | 291 us | 98 us | 2.98x |

### RADV BDA vs AMDGPU AQL/PM4 ABABA

The ABABA benchmark records 10K alternating dispatches across two
pipelines with 100 binding-table entries and a 20% overlap grouping
pattern. It is designed to stress replay, binding publication, and
driver/device drain behavior instead of a single homogeneous pipeline
loop.

| Path | Submit-only | Submit + wait | Interpretation |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Vulkan BDA on RADV | 36.288 us | 47.190 ms | HAL-side replay is cheap,
but public Vulkan/RADV drains the alternating-pipeline sequence slowly.
|
| AMDGPU AQL dynamic | 138.183 us | 41.484 ms | Low host submit cost,
but device drain still follows AQL packet-stream behavior. |
| AMDGPU AQL static | 98.677 us | 41.075 ms | Static publication helps
submit, while drain remains AQL-like. |
| AMDGPU PM4 static | 1.445 us | 5.076 ms | One resident PM4 IB packet
gives the lowest submit cost and much lower drain time. |
| AMDGPU PM4 fixup | 7.658 us | 5.194 ms | Dynamic binding-table update
via GPU fixup plus PM4 IB replay stays close to static PM4. |

This is the backend mechanism comparison. Vulkan BDA gets the Vulkan HAL
out of descriptor emulation and into native replay. AMDGPU PM4 shows the
next layer: when the backend owns the low-level command stream below the
public driver API, the same recorded-work shape can drain far faster.
This is also a useful RADV-vs-PM4 ABABA contrast: the HAL-side Vulkan
replay is already cheaper than AQL submit, while PM4 shows what the
device-side alternating-pipeline ABABA drain can look like when the
backend bypasses the public Vulkan driver stack.

The long RADV ABABA drain is not a regression in the HAL barrier
lowering. A profiled ABABA run recorded one queue-device interval of
roughly 40 ms for the same 10K alternating-dispatch sequence, while the
host submit-to-ready span was only a few milliseconds. The
command-buffer metadata showed the expected 10K alternating dispatches
and execution-only barriers, and the sync2 lowering now preserves
execution ordering without synthesizing memory read/write visibility.

## Highlights

This rewrite turns Vulkan from a synchronous, descriptor-heavy
compatibility backend into a modern HAL backend:

- asynchronous queue semantics using timeline-semaphore epochs and
explicit frontiers;
- native queue paths for transfer, dispatch, file staging, sparse
binding, command-buffer execute, and host calls;
- descriptor ABI compatibility plus a BDA ABI that materially improves
command-buffer replay scaling;
- reusable native Vulkan command-buffer replay for BDA dispatches;
- HAL-native queue, command-buffer, executable, and dispatch profiling
through `iree-profile`;
- queryable backend statistics for replay, BDA publication, and
timestamp caches;
- stricter unsupported-case handling instead of compatibility-shaped
silent fallback behavior;
- No more C++.

TLDR: the descriptor compatibility path is already materially better
than old Vulkan, the BDA path is the intended fast path and gives Vulkan
native command-buffer replay instead of deferred HAL replay, direct
transfers no longer bounce through emulated command buffers, and the
backend now has the profiling/statistics hooks needed to keep tightening
the hot paths with hard evidence.

commit_message:
[Vulkan] HAL Rewrite (#24459)

This should be compatible with old VMFBs. I expect some platforms to
possibly need feature backfill or compatibility support but our testing
story is too thin to know yet. The big shift here is baselining on
Vulkan 1.3. With a bit of extra work we could stretch back to 1.2 with
extensions.

---

This PR replaces the legacy Vulkan HAL with a new implementation built
around the current HAL queue contract, native Vulkan command recording,
explicit feature negotiation, buffer-device-address dispatch, direct
transfer/file paths, and HAL-native profiling.

The old driver worked (and was some of the oldest IREE code, written
before it was even open sourced!), but it grew around synchronous
submission, descriptor-set dispatch, and direct recording assumptions
that do not map well to modern IREE workloads. In particular, it did not
give us a clean way to model asynchronous queue frontiers, reusable
command-buffer replay, file/transfer operations, BDA dispatch, or
backend-visible profiling statistics without continuing to layer
compatibility paths on top of the old design.

The new driver has two goals:

- Keep descriptor ABI compatibility for existing Vulkan executables.
- Make the optimized Vulkan path descriptor-free, replayable,
observable, and aligned with the same command-buffer model used by newer
HAL backends.

## Driver Architecture

The implementation is organized around explicit ownership boundaries:

- `api.*` defines Vulkan HAL feature policy, extension names, and public
option translation.
- `physical_device.*` owns enumeration, device snapshots, baseline
validation, extension discovery, feature/property capture, and
queue-family description.
- `logical_device.*` owns logical-device creation, queue selection,
topology, allocator installation, executable-cache creation, file
import, and device queries.
- `queue.*` owns queue submission, timeline epochs, dependency
resolution, native command-buffer allocation, asynchronous completion,
staging, direct dispatch, transfer/file operation recording, profiling
timestamps, and replay cache statistics.
- `command_buffer.*` owns reusable HAL command-buffer storage, compact
command records, descriptor/BDA requirement accounting, resource
lifetime tracking, and native replay into `VkCommandBuffer`.
- `executable.*` owns Vulkan executable loading, SPIR-V module/pipeline
creation, descriptor ABI metadata, BDA ABI metadata, raw BDA executable
support, global lookup, and per-pipeline dispatch metadata.

Unsupported cases are rejected at the boundary where they are
discovered. The rewrite intentionally avoids silent fallbacks that would
hide missing Vulkan features or route hot paths through emulation.

## Queue Model

The new queue implementation uses Vulkan timeline semaphores as queue
epochs. Each selected queue lane tracks accepted submissions,
signal/wait frontiers, completion state, and pending cleanup. HAL
semaphore dependencies are resolved through the queue path without
assuming FIFO submission order.

Queue submission supports:

- execution barriers;
- queue allocation and deallocation;
- sparse binding;
- fill, update, copy, read, and write operations;
- direct dispatch;
- reusable command-buffer execute;
- file-backed staging;
- host callbacks.

This replaces the old split between synchronous direct operations and
special driver-side helper paths. Queue work now enters through one
scheduling model and retires through one completion model.

## Executable And Dispatch ABIs

The driver supports both Vulkan executable ABIs:

- `vulkan-spirv-fb`, the descriptor ABI, for compatibility with existing
descriptor-set storage-buffer executables.
- `vulkan-spirv-bda-v1` and `vulkan-spirv-bda-raw`, the BDA ABIs, for
descriptor-free dispatch through a device-address binding table.

The descriptor ABI now uses `VK_KHR_push_descriptor` when the device
supports it and the pipeline layout fits the extension limits. That
removes descriptor pool allocation and descriptor-set update overhead
from the descriptor compatibility path.

BDA is the primary performance path. The runtime publishes a compact
device-address binding table and the shader reads resource addresses
directly. Reusable command buffers can keep the native Vulkan command
body resident while only the published BDA table bytes change between
executions.

## Device Compatibility

This rewrite intentionally raises the Vulkan baseline. The
driver-created instance requests Vulkan 1.3 by default, and
physical-device enumeration only accepts devices with:

- `apiVersion >= VK_API_VERSION_1_3`;
- `timelineSemaphore`;
- `scalarBlockLayout`;
- `synchronization2`;
- at least one compute-capable queue family.

That baseline is what lets the queue use timeline-semaphore epochs,
express barriers through synchronization2, and keep shader/storage
layouts consistent without carrying old synchronization and layout
compatibility paths. The target is Vulkan 1.3, not Vulkan 1.4; Vulkan
1.3 has been the stable modern Vulkan baseline since [January
2022](https://docs.vulkan.org/guide/latest/versions.html#vulkan-13-features-breakdown).

`bufferDeviceAddress` is a second gate for the optimized BDA dispatch
ABI. A device can still use descriptor-ABI executables without BDA, but
`vulkan-spirv-bda-v1` and `vulkan-spirv-bda-raw` require BDA because
their binding table is a table of device addresses instead of descriptor
bindings.

Optional capabilities remain opportunistic:

- `VK_KHR_push_descriptor` accelerates the descriptor compatibility path
when available.
- `VK_EXT_calibrated_timestamps` improves profile clock correlation when
available.
- external memory, host memory import, sparse binding, and sparse
residency are enabled only when the device and requested HAL features
require them.

As a rough ecosystem sanity check, the [Vulkan Hardware Database
`apiVersion`
distribution](https://vulkan.gpuinfo.org/displaycoreproperty.php?name=apiversion)
reports Vulkan 1.3 or 1.4 in 24,376 of 44,893 submitted all-platform
reports (54.3%). The desktop slice is stronger: 12,446 of 19,758
[Windows
reports](https://vulkan.gpuinfo.org/displaycoreproperty.php?name=apiversion&platform=windows)
(63.0%) and 9,547 of 15,964 [Linux
reports](https://vulkan.gpuinfo.org/displaycoreproperty.php?name=apiversion&platform=linux)
(59.8%) are Vulkan 1.3+. Android is lower at 2,400 of 7,832 [Android
reports](https://vulkan.gpuinfo.org/displaycoreproperty.php?name=apiversion&platform=android)
(30.6%), which matches the fact that this rewrite is primarily aimed at
modern desktop/server Vulkan rather than old mobile Vulkan stacks.

The required feature bits are not the practical compatibility cliff
within the modern driver cohort: gpuinfo.org's all-platform [Vulkan 1.2
feature coverage](https://vulkan.gpuinfo.org/listfeaturescore12.php) and
[Vulkan 1.3 feature
coverage](https://vulkan.gpuinfo.org/listfeaturescore13.php) list
`timelineSemaphore` at 99.88%, `scalarBlockLayout` at 98.82%,
`synchronization2` at 99.82%, and `bufferDeviceAddress` at 98.47%. Treat
those numbers as [community-submitted device/report coverage rather than
market share](https://vulkan.gpuinfo.org/about.php), but they are useful
evidence that the meaningful bump is the Vulkan 1.3 driver baseline, not
an obscure optional-feature combination.

## Command Buffers

HAL command buffers record structured Vulkan command records instead of
trying to expose old direct-command-buffer behavior through the HAL API.
During recording the driver accumulates:

- descriptor requirements for descriptor ABI replay;
- BDA publication byte requirements for BDA replay;
- retained resources for safe command-buffer lifetime;
- dispatch metadata required for profiling and native replay.

At queue execution time the command buffer is replayed into a native
`VkCommandBuffer`. BDA command buffers can use the native replay cache:
the cache keeps reusable native command buffers and BDA publication
storage per queue lane, skips publication when binding slots are
unchanged, and exposes
hits, misses, forks, bypasses, trims, peak instance count, and peak
publication bytes through `query_i64` counters under
`vulkan.queue.native_replay_cache`.

Descriptor command buffers currently bypass native replay caching
because their replayed Vulkan commands embed binding-table-dependent
descriptor state. This matches the old indirect-command-buffer shape:
the old driver recorded deferred HAL commands for binding-table command
buffers and materialized a native Vulkan command buffer during each
`queue_execute`. The rewrite keeps that compatibility contract, uses
push descriptors when available, and reserves resident native replay for
BDA command buffers where the command body is independent of the
execute-time binding table.

## Transfer And File Paths

Queue transfers are native Vulkan operations in the new driver. Fill,
update, and copy are recorded directly into Vulkan command buffers.
Unaligned fill and update edges are patched with driver-owned built-in
pipelines instead of falling through an emulated transfer layer.

File reads and writes use storage-buffer-backed files directly when
available. Host-backed files are staged through device-visible memory
and the async file path, keeping file operations on the same
queue/completion model as the rest of the driver.

## Profiling And Statistics

Profiling is built into the queue and command-buffer paths. The driver
records HAL executable metadata, command-buffer metadata, queue events,
queue device timestamps, and optional per-dispatch timestamp ranges
through the local HAL profile recorder used by `iree-profile`.

Timestamp query pools are queue-owned and cached. Calibrated timestamp
support is used when available to relate Vulkan device ticks to the HAL
profile timeline, and invalid calibrated ranges are marked instead of
forcing a bad clock fit.

The driver also exposes backend statistics through device queries,
including native replay cache behavior, BDA publication cache behavior,
and timestamp query cache behavior. These counters make performance
paths inspectable instead of requiring driver-internal debugging.

## Performance Characterization

The performance goal of the rewrite is simple: Vulkan command buffers
should be cheap to submit because the backend records native Vulkan work
once and replays that work directly. The benchmark rows below keep that
contract visible by separating host submit cost from end-to-end drain
cost:

- Submit-only rows time command-buffer replay and queue submission, with
the final completion wait outside the timed region.
- Submit + wait rows include the final completion wait and therefore
include driver and device drain behavior.

All rows are release Google Benchmark medians. The benchmark set
compares the old descriptor-set Vulkan HAL, the new
descriptor-compatible Vulkan path, the new BDA Vulkan dispatch ABI, and
AMDGPU AQL/PM4 command-buffer replay. Those are distinct mechanisms, so
the tables keep them separate instead of turning the result into a
single backend ranking.

### Vulkan Command-Buffer Replay

Homogeneous 10K-dispatch command-buffer replay:

| Path | ABI | Submit-only | Submit + wait | Interpretation |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Old Vulkan HAL | Descriptor sets | 5.139 ms | 5.609 ms | Deferred HAL
command buffer replayed into Vulkan and bound descriptor sets for every
dispatch. |
| New Vulkan HAL | Push descriptors | 2.072 ms | 5.257 ms | Descriptor

cost by 2.48x. |
| New Vulkan HAL | BDA | 12.361 us | 1.435 ms | Native BDA replay hits
the native replay cache and cuts host replay cost by 416x vs old Vulkan.
|

For command-buffer recording, the hot unvalidated/unretained path

| Path | Recording mode | 5K-dispatch record-only |
| --- | --- | ---: |
| Old Vulkan HAL | Default validation/retention | 183.547 us |
| Old Vulkan HAL | Unvalidated + unretained | 93.925 us |
| New Vulkan HAL | Default validation/retention | 207.266 us |
| New Vulkan HAL | Unvalidated, retained | 113.191 us |
| New Vulkan HAL | Validated, unretained | 190.903 us |
| New Vulkan HAL | Unvalidated + unretained | 97.998 us |

Queue transfer operations now go through native queue paths instead of

| Operation | Size | Old Vulkan submit-only | New Vulkan submit-only |
Speedup |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Copy batch x20 | 4 B | 304 us | 46 us | 6.54x |
| Copy batch x20 | 4 KiB | 309 us | 57 us | 5.47x |
| Fill batch x20 | 4 B | 295 us | 48 us | 6.09x |
| Fill batch x20 | 4 KiB | 285 us | 57 us | 5.02x |
| Update batch x20 | 4 B | 278 us | 59 us | 4.75x |
| Update batch x20 | 4 KiB | 291 us | 98 us | 2.98x |

| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |

| AMDGPU AQL static | 98.677 us | 41.075 ms | Static publication helps

| AMDGPU PM4 static | 1.445 us | 5.076 ms | One resident PM4 IB packet
gives the lowest submit cost and much lower drain time. |

commit_message:
[Vulkan] HAL Rewrite (#24459)

This should be compatible with old VMFBs. I expect some platforms to
possibly need feature backfill or compatibility support but our testing
story is too thin to know yet. The big shift here is baselining on
Vulkan 1.3. With a bit of extra work we could stretch back to 1.2 with
extensions.

---

This PR replaces the legacy Vulkan HAL with a new implementation built
around the current HAL queue contract, native Vulkan command recording,
explicit feature negotiation, buffer-device-address dispatch, direct
transfer/file paths, and HAL-native profiling.

The old driver worked (and was some of the oldest IREE code, written
before it was even open sourced!), but it grew around synchronous
submission, descriptor-set dispatch, and direct recording assumptions
that do not map well to modern IREE workloads. In particular, it did not
give us a clean way to model asynchronous queue frontiers, reusable
command-buffer replay, file/transfer operations, BDA dispatch, or
backend-visible profiling statistics without continuing to layer
compatibility paths on top of the old design.

The new driver has two goals:

- Keep descriptor ABI compatibility for existing Vulkan executables.
- Make the optimized Vulkan path descriptor-free, replayable,
observable, and aligned with the same command-buffer model used by newer
HAL backends.

## Driver Architecture

The implementation is organized around explicit ownership boundaries:

- `api.*` defines Vulkan HAL feature policy, extension names, and public
option translation.
- `physical_device.*` owns enumeration, device snapshots, baseline
validation, extension discovery, feature/property capture, and
queue-family description.
- `logical_device.*` owns logical-device creation, queue selection,
topology, allocator installation, executable-cache creation, file
import, and device queries.
- `queue.*` owns queue submission, timeline epochs, dependency
resolution, native command-buffer allocation, asynchronous completion,
staging, direct dispatch, transfer/file operation recording, profiling
timestamps, and replay cache statistics.
- `command_buffer.*` owns reusable HAL command-buffer storage, compact
command records, descriptor/BDA requirement accounting, resource
lifetime tracking, and native replay into `VkCommandBuffer`.
- `executable.*` owns Vulkan executable loading, SPIR-V module/pipeline
creation, descriptor ABI metadata, BDA ABI metadata, raw BDA executable
support, global lookup, and per-pipeline dispatch metadata.

Unsupported cases are rejected at the boundary where they are
discovered. The rewrite intentionally avoids silent fallbacks that would
hide missing Vulkan features or route hot paths through emulation.

## Queue Model

The new queue implementation uses Vulkan timeline semaphores as queue
epochs. Each selected queue lane tracks accepted submissions,
signal/wait frontiers, completion state, and pending cleanup. HAL
semaphore dependencies are resolved through the queue path without
assuming FIFO submission order.

Queue submission supports:

- execution barriers;
- queue allocation and deallocation;
- sparse binding;
- fill, update, copy, read, and write operations;
- direct dispatch;
- reusable command-buffer execute;
- file-backed staging;
- host callbacks.

This replaces the old split between synchronous direct operations and
special driver-side helper paths. Queue work now enters through one
scheduling model and retires through one completion model.

## Executable And Dispatch ABIs

The driver supports both Vulkan executable ABIs:

- `vulkan-spirv-fb`, the descriptor ABI, for compatibility with existing
descriptor-set storage-buffer executables.
- `vulkan-spirv-bda-v1` and `vulkan-spirv-bda-raw`, the BDA ABIs, for
descriptor-free dispatch through a device-address binding table.

The descriptor ABI now uses `VK_KHR_push_descriptor` when the device
supports it and the pipeline layout fits the extension limits. That
removes descriptor pool allocation and descriptor-set update overhead
from the descriptor compatibility path.

BDA is the primary performance path. The runtime publishes a compact
device-address binding table and the shader reads resource addresses
directly. Reusable command buffers can keep the native Vulkan command
body resident while only the published BDA table bytes change between
executions.

## Device Compatibility

This rewrite intentionally raises the Vulkan baseline. The
driver-created instance requests Vulkan 1.3 by default, and
physical-device enumeration only accepts devices with:

- `apiVersion >= VK_API_VERSION_1_3`;
- `timelineSemaphore`;
- `scalarBlockLayout`;
- `synchronization2`;
- at least one compute-capable queue family.

That baseline is what lets the queue use timeline-semaphore epochs,
express barriers through synchronization2, and keep shader/storage
layouts consistent without carrying old synchronization and layout
compatibility paths. The target is Vulkan 1.3, not Vulkan 1.4; Vulkan
1.3 has been the stable modern Vulkan baseline since [January
2022](https://docs.vulkan.org/guide/latest/versions.html#vulkan-13-features-breakdown).

`bufferDeviceAddress` is a second gate for the optimized BDA dispatch
ABI. A device can still use descriptor-ABI executables without BDA, but
`vulkan-spirv-bda-v1` and `vulkan-spirv-bda-raw` require BDA because
their binding table is a table of device addresses instead of descriptor
bindings.

Optional capabilities remain opportunistic:

- `VK_KHR_push_descriptor` accelerates the descriptor compatibility path
when available.
- `VK_EXT_calibrated_timestamps` improves profile clock correlation when
available.
- external memory, host memory import, sparse binding, and sparse
residency are enabled only when the device and requested HAL features
require them.

As a rough ecosystem sanity check, the [Vulkan Hardware Database
`apiVersion`
distribution](https://vulkan.gpuinfo.org/displaycoreproperty.php?name=apiversion)
reports Vulkan 1.3 or 1.4 in 24,376 of 44,893 submitted all-platform
reports (54.3%). The desktop slice is stronger: 12,446 of 19,758
[Windows
reports](https://vulkan.gpuinfo.org/displaycoreproperty.php?name=apiversion&platform=windows)
(63.0%) and 9,547 of 15,964 [Linux
reports](https://vulkan.gpuinfo.org/displaycoreproperty.php?name=apiversion&platform=linux)
(59.8%) are Vulkan 1.3+. Android is lower at 2,400 of 7,832 [Android
reports](https://vulkan.gpuinfo.org/displaycoreproperty.php?name=apiversion&platform=android)
(30.6%), which matches the fact that this rewrite is primarily aimed at
modern desktop/server Vulkan rather than old mobile Vulkan stacks.

The required feature bits are not the practical compatibility cliff
within the modern driver cohort: gpuinfo.org's all-platform [Vulkan 1.2
feature coverage](https://vulkan.gpuinfo.org/listfeaturescore12.php) and
[Vulkan 1.3 feature
coverage](https://vulkan.gpuinfo.org/listfeaturescore13.php) list
`timelineSemaphore` at 99.88%, `scalarBlockLayout` at 98.82%,
`synchronization2` at 99.82%, and `bufferDeviceAddress` at 98.47%. Treat
those numbers as [community-submitted device/report coverage rather than
market share](https://vulkan.gpuinfo.org/about.php), but they are useful
evidence that the meaningful bump is the Vulkan 1.3 driver baseline, not
an obscure optional-feature combination.

## Command Buffers

HAL command buffers record structured Vulkan command records instead of
trying to expose old direct-command-buffer behavior through the HAL API.
During recording the driver accumulates:

- descriptor requirements for descriptor ABI replay;
- BDA publication byte requirements for BDA replay;
- retained resources for safe command-buffer lifetime;
- dispatch metadata required for profiling and native replay.

At queue execution time the command buffer is replayed into a native
`VkCommandBuffer`. BDA command buffers can use the native replay cache:
the cache keeps reusable native command buffers and BDA publication
storage per queue lane, skips publication when binding slots are
unchanged, and exposes
hits, misses, forks, bypasses, trims, peak instance count, and peak
publication bytes through `query_i64` counters under
`vulkan.queue.native_replay_cache`.

Descriptor command buffers currently bypass native replay caching
because their replayed Vulkan commands embed binding-table-dependent
descriptor state. This matches the old indirect-command-buffer shape:
the old driver recorded deferred HAL commands for binding-table command
buffers and materialized a native Vulkan command buffer during each
`queue_execute`. The rewrite keeps that compatibility contract, uses
push descriptors when available, and reserves resident native replay for
BDA command buffers where the command body is independent of the
execute-time binding table.

## Transfer And File Paths

Queue transfers are native Vulkan operations in the new driver. Fill,
update, and copy are recorded directly into Vulkan command buffers.
Unaligned fill and update edges are patched with driver-owned built-in
pipelines instead of falling through an emulated transfer layer.

File reads and writes use storage-buffer-backed files directly when
available. Host-backed files are staged through device-visible memory
and the async file path, keeping file operations on the same
queue/completion model as the rest of the driver.

## Profiling And Statistics

Profiling is built into the queue and command-buffer paths. The driver
records HAL executable metadata, command-buffer metadata, queue events,
queue device timestamps, and optional per-dispatch timestamp ranges
through the local HAL profile recorder used by `iree-profile`.

Timestamp query pools are queue-owned and cached. Calibrated timestamp
support is used when available to relate Vulkan device ticks to the HAL
profile timeline, and invalid calibrated ranges are marked instead of
forcing a bad clock fit.

The driver also exposes backend statistics through device queries,
including native replay cache behavior, BDA publication cache behavior,
and timestamp query cache behavior. These counters make performance
paths inspectable instead of requiring driver-internal debugging.

## Performance Characterization

The performance goal of the rewrite is simple: Vulkan command buffers
should be cheap to submit because the backend records native Vulkan work
once and replays that work directly. The benchmark rows below keep that
contract visible by separating host submit cost from end-to-end drain
cost:

- Submit-only rows time command-buffer replay and queue submission, with
the final completion wait outside the timed region.
- Submit + wait rows include the final completion wait and therefore
include driver and device drain behavior.

All rows are release Google Benchmark medians. The benchmark set
compares the old descriptor-set Vulkan HAL, the new
descriptor-compatible Vulkan path, the new BDA Vulkan dispatch ABI, and
AMDGPU AQL/PM4 command-buffer replay. Those are distinct mechanisms, so
the tables keep them separate instead of turning the result into a
single backend ranking.

### Vulkan Command-Buffer Replay

Homogeneous 10K-dispatch command-buffer replay:

| Path | ABI | Submit-only | Submit + wait | Interpretation |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Old Vulkan HAL | Descriptor sets | 5.139 ms | 5.609 ms | Deferred HAL
command buffer replayed into Vulkan and bound descriptor sets for every
dispatch. |
| New Vulkan HAL | Push descriptors | 2.072 ms | 5.257 ms | Descriptor
compatibility path avoids descriptor pool/set churn and cuts host replay
cost by 2.48x. |
| New Vulkan HAL | BDA | 12.361 us | 1.435 ms | Native BDA replay hits
the native replay cache and cuts host replay cost by 416x vs old Vulkan.
|

The descriptor row is the compatibility story: the new HAL is still
faster than old Vulkan when running the legacy descriptor ABI. The BDA
row is the design story: when the compiler targets the new ABI, replay
becomes one cached native command-buffer submission instead of a
per-dispatch descriptor-binding loop.

For command-buffer recording, the hot unvalidated/unretained path
remains close to the old implementation, and the default checked path is
now within about 24 us over 5K dispatches:

| Path | Recording mode | 5K-dispatch record-only |
| --- | --- | ---: |
| Old Vulkan HAL | Default validation/retention | 183.547 us |
| Old Vulkan HAL | Unvalidated + unretained | 93.925 us |
| New Vulkan HAL | Default validation/retention | 207.266 us |
| New Vulkan HAL | Unvalidated, retained | 113.191 us |
| New Vulkan HAL | Validated, unretained | 190.903 us |
| New Vulkan HAL | Unvalidated + unretained | 97.998 us |

That distinction matters for interpreting the submit rows. The rewrite
is not winning by making unchecked recording magically cheaper; it is
winning because recorded BDA command buffers replay as native Vulkan
work instead of walking the IREE deferred command stream on every
submission. The record-only default delta is validation and retention
bookkeeping on a cold path; the repeated-use win is in the submit/replay
path.

### Direct Transfer Host Cost

Queue transfer operations now go through native queue paths instead of
the old host-side emulated command-buffer path. The strong claim here is
submit-only host overhead:

| Operation | Size | Old Vulkan submit-only | New Vulkan submit-only |
Speedup |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Copy batch x20 | 4 B | 304 us | 46 us | 6.54x |
| Copy batch x20 | 4 KiB | 309 us | 57 us | 5.47x |
| Fill batch x20 | 4 B | 295 us | 48 us | 6.09x |
| Fill batch x20 | 4 KiB | 285 us | 57 us | 5.02x |
| Update batch x20 | 4 B | 278 us | 59 us | 4.75x |
| Update batch x20 | 4 KiB | 291 us | 98 us | 2.98x |

### RADV BDA vs AMDGPU AQL/PM4 ABABA

The ABABA benchmark records 10K alternating dispatches across two
pipelines with 100 binding-table entries and a 20% overlap grouping
pattern. It is designed to stress replay, binding publication, and
driver/device drain behavior instead of a single homogeneous pipeline
loop.

| Path | Submit-only | Submit + wait | Interpretation |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Vulkan BDA on RADV | 36.288 us | 47.190 ms | HAL-side replay is cheap,
but public Vulkan/RADV drains the alternating-pipeline sequence slowly.
|
| AMDGPU AQL dynamic | 138.183 us | 41.484 ms | Low host submit cost,
but device drain still follows AQL packet-stream behavior. |
| AMDGPU AQL static | 98.677 us | 41.075 ms | Static publication helps
submit, while drain remains AQL-like. |
| AMDGPU PM4 static | 1.445 us | 5.076 ms | One resident PM4 IB packet
gives the lowest submit cost and much lower drain time. |
| AMDGPU PM4 fixup | 7.658 us | 5.194 ms | Dynamic binding-table update
via GPU fixup plus PM4 IB replay stays close to static PM4. |

This is the backend mechanism comparison. Vulkan BDA gets the Vulkan HAL
out of descriptor emulation and into native replay. AMDGPU PM4 shows the
next layer: when the backend owns the low-level command stream below the
public driver API, the same recorded-work shape can drain far faster.
This is also a useful RADV-vs-PM4 ABABA contrast: the HAL-side Vulkan
replay is already cheaper than AQL submit, while PM4 shows what the
device-side alternating-pipeline ABABA drain can look like when the
backend bypasses the public Vulkan driver stack.

The long RADV ABABA drain is not a regression in the HAL barrier
lowering. A profiled ABABA run recorded one queue-device interval of
roughly 40 ms for the same 10K alternating-dispatch sequence, while the
host submit-to-ready span was only a few milliseconds. The

before it was even open sourced!), but it grew around synchronous
submission, descriptor-set dispatch, and direct recording assumptions

backend-visible profiling statistics without continuing to layer
compatibility paths on top of the old design.

- Keep descriptor ABI compatibility for existing Vulkan executables.

- `api.*` defines Vulkan HAL feature policy, extension names, and public
option translation.
- `physical_device.*` owns enumeration, device snapshots, baseline
validation, extension discovery, feature/property capture, and

topology, allocator installation, executable-cache creation, file
import, and device queries.

staging, direct dispatch, transfer/file operation recording, profiling
timestamps, and replay cache statistics.
- `command_buffer.*` owns reusable HAL command-buffer storage, compact
command records, descriptor/BDA requirement accounting, resource
lifetime tracking, and native replay into `VkCommandBuffer`.
- `executable.*` owns Vulkan executable loading, SPIR-V module/pipeline

discovered. The rewrite intentionally avoids silent fallbacks that would
hide missing Vulkan features or route hot paths through emulation.

The new queue implementation uses Vulkan timeline semaphores as queue

assuming FIFO submission order.

- execution barriers;
- queue allocation and deallocation;
- sparse binding;
- fill, update, copy, read, and write operations;
- direct dispatch;
- reusable command-buffer execute;
- file-backed staging;
- host callbacks.

descriptor-set storage-buffer executables.
- `vulkan-spirv-bda-v1` and `vulkan-spirv-bda-raw`, the BDA ABIs, for

removes descriptor pool allocation and descriptor-set update overhead
from the descriptor compatibility path.

directly. Reusable command buffers can keep the native Vulkan command
body resident while only the published BDA table bytes change between
executions.

bindings.

when available.

available.

coverage](https://vulkan.gpuinfo.org/listfeaturescore13.php) list
`timelineSemaphore` at 99.88%, `scalarBlockLayout` at 98.82%,
`synchronization2` at 99.82%, and `bufferDeviceAddress` at 98.47%. Treat
those numbers as [community-submitted device/report coverage rather than
market share](https://vulkan.gpuinfo.org/about.php), but they are useful
evidence that the meaningful bump is the Vulkan 1.3 driver baseline, not
an obscure optional-feature combination.

## Command Buffers

HAL command buffers record structured Vulkan command records instead of
trying to expose old direct-command-buffer behavior through the HAL API.
During recording the driver accumulates:

- descriptor requirements for descriptor ABI replay;
- BDA publication byte requirements for BDA replay;
- retained resources for safe command-buffer lifetime;
- dispatch metadata required for profiling and native replay.

At queue execution time the command buffer is replayed into a native
`VkCommandBuffer`. BDA command buffers can use the native replay cache:
the cache keeps reusable native command buffers and BDA publication
storage per queue lane, skips publication when binding slots are
unchanged, and exposes
hits, misses, forks, bypasses, trims, peak instance count, and peak
publication bytes through `query_i64` counters under
`vulkan.queue.native_replay_cache`.

Descriptor command buffers currently bypass native replay caching
because their replayed Vulkan commands embed binding-table-dependent
descriptor state. This matches the old indirect-command-buffer shape:
the old driver recorded deferred HAL commands for binding-table command
buffers and materialized a native Vulkan command buffer during each
`queue_execute`. The rewrite keeps that compatibility contract, uses
push descriptors when available, and reserves resident native replay for
BDA command buffers where the command body is independent of the
execute-time binding table.

## Transfer And File Paths

Queue transfers are native Vulkan operations in the new driver. Fill,
update, and copy are recorded directly into Vulkan command buffers.
Unaligned fill and update edges are patched with driver-owned built-in
pipelines instead of falling through an emulated transfer layer.

File reads and writes use storage-buffer-backed files directly when
available. Host-backed files are staged through device-visible memory
and the async file path, keeping file operations on the same
queue/completion model as the rest of the driver.

## Profiling And Statistics

Profiling is built into the queue and command-buffer paths. The driver
records HAL executable metadata, command-buffer metadata, queue events,
queue device timestamps, and optional per-dispatch timestamp ranges
through the local HAL profile recorder used by `iree-profile`.

Timestamp query pools are queue-owned and cached. Calibrated timestamp
support is used when available to relate Vulkan device ticks to the HAL
profile timeline, and invalid calibrated ranges are marked instead of
forcing a bad clock fit.

The driver also exposes backend statistics through device queries,
including native replay cache behavior, BDA publication cache behavior,
and timestamp query cache behavior. These counters make performance
paths inspectable instead of requiring driver-internal debugging.

## Performance Characterization

The performance goal of the rewrite is simple: Vulkan command buffers
should be cheap to submit because the backend records native Vulkan work
once and replays that work directly. The benchmark rows below keep that
contract visible by separating host submit cost from end-to-end drain
cost:

- Submit-only rows time command-buffer replay and queue submission, with
the final completion wait outside the timed region.
- Submit + wait rows include the final completion wait and therefore
include driver and device drain behavior.

All rows are release Google Benchmark medians. The benchmark set
compares the old descriptor-set Vulkan HAL, the new
descriptor-compatible Vulkan path, the new BDA Vulkan dispatch ABI, and
AMDGPU AQL/PM4 command-buffer replay. Those are distinct mechanisms, so
the tables keep them separate instead of turning the result into a
single backend ranking.

### Vulkan Command-Buffer Replay

Homogeneous 10K-dispatch command-buffer replay:

| Path | ABI | Submit-only | Submit + wait | Interpretation |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Old Vulkan HAL | Descriptor sets | 5.139 ms | 5.609 ms | Deferred HAL
command buffer replayed into Vulkan and bound descriptor sets for every
dispatch. |
| New Vulkan HAL | Push descriptors | 2.072 ms | 5.257 ms | Descriptor
compatibility path avoids descriptor pool/set churn and cuts host replay
cost by 2.48x. |
| New Vulkan HAL | BDA | 12.361 us | 1.435 ms | Native BDA replay hits
the native replay cache and cuts host replay cost by 416x vs old Vulkan.
|

The descriptor row is the compatibility story: the new HAL is still
faster than old Vulkan when running the legacy descriptor ABI. The BDA
row is the design story: when the compiler targets the new ABI, replay
becomes one cached native command-buffer submission instead of a
per-dispatch descriptor-binding loop.

For command-buffer recording, the hot unvalidated/unretained path
remains close to the old implementation, and the default checked path is
now within about 24 us over 5K dispatches:

| Path | Recording mode | 5K-dispatch record-only |
| --- | --- | ---: |
| Old Vulkan HAL | Default validation/retention | 183.547 us |
| Old Vulkan HAL | Unvalidated + unretained | 93.925 us |
| New Vulkan HAL | Default validation/retention | 207.266 us |
| New Vulkan HAL | Unvalidated, retained | 113.191 us |
| New Vulkan HAL | Validated, unretained | 190.903 us |
| New Vulkan HAL | Unvalidated + unretained | 97.998 us |

That distinction matters for interpreting the submit rows. The rewrite
is not winning by making unchecked recording magically cheaper; it is
winning because recorded BDA command buffers replay as native Vulkan
work instead of walking the IREE deferred command stream on every
submission. The record-only default delta is validation and retention
bookkeeping on a cold path; the repeated-use win is in the submit/replay
path.

### Direct Transfer Host Cost

Queue transfer operations now go through native queue paths instead of
the old host-side emulated command-buffer path. The strong claim here is
submit-only host overhead:

| Operation | Size | Old Vulkan submit-only | New Vulkan submit-only |
Speedup |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Copy batch x20 | 4 B | 304 us | 46 us | 6.54x |
| Copy batch x20 | 4 KiB | 309 us | 57 us | 5.47x |
| Fill batch x20 | 4 B | 295 us | 48 us | 6.09x |
| Fill batch x20 | 4 KiB | 285 us | 57 us | 5.02x |
| Update batch x20 | 4 B | 278 us | 59 us | 4.75x |
| Update batch x20 | 4 KiB | 291 us | 98 us | 2.98x |

### RADV BDA vs AMDGPU AQL/PM4 ABABA

The ABABA benchmark records 10K alternating dispatches across two
pipelines with 100 binding-table entries and a 20% overlap grouping
pattern. It is designed to stress replay, binding publication, and
driver/device drain behavior instead of a single homogeneous pipeline
loop.

| Path | Submit-only | Submit + wait | Interpretation |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Vulkan BDA on RADV | 36.288 us | 47.190 ms | HAL-side replay is cheap,
but public Vulkan/RADV drains the alternating-pipeline sequence slowly.
|
| AMDGPU AQL dynamic | 138.183 us | 41.484 ms | Low host submit cost,
but device drain still follows AQL packet-stream behavior. |
| AMDGPU AQL static | 98.677 us | 41.075 ms | Static publication helps
submit, while drain remains AQL-like. |
| AMDGPU PM4 static | 1.445 us | 5.076 ms | One resident PM4 IB packet
gives the lowest submit cost and much lower drain time. |
| AMDGPU PM4 fixup | 7.658 us | 5.194 ms | Dynamic binding-table update
via GPU fixup plus PM4 IB replay stays close to static PM4. |

This is the backend mechanism comparison. Vulkan BDA gets the Vulkan HAL
out of descriptor emulation and into native replay. AMDGPU PM4 shows the
next layer: when the backend owns the low-level command stream below the
public driver API, the same recorded-work shape can drain far faster.
This is also a useful RADV-vs-PM4 ABABA contrast: the HAL-side Vulkan
replay is already cheaper than AQL submit, while PM4 shows what the
device-side alternating-pipeline ABABA drain can look like when the
backend bypasses the public Vulkan driver stack.

The long RADV ABABA drain is not a regression in the HAL barrier
lowering. A profiled ABABA run recorded one queue-device interval of
roughly 40 ms for the same 10K alternating-dispatch sequence, while the
host submit-to-ready span was only a few milliseconds. The
command-buffer metadata showed the expected 10K alternating dispatches
and execution-only barriers, and the sync2 lowering now preserves
execution ordering without synthesizing memory read/write visibility.

## Highlights

This rewrite turns Vulkan from a synchronous, descriptor-heavy
compatibility backend into a modern HAL backend:

- asynchronous queue semantics using timeline-semaphore epochs and
explicit frontiers;
- native queue paths for transfer, dispatch, file staging, sparse
binding, command-buffer execute, and host calls;
- descriptor ABI compatibility plus a BDA ABI that materially improves
command-buffer replay scaling;
- reusable native Vulkan command-buffer replay for BDA dispatches;
- HAL-native queue, command-buffer, executable, and dispatch profiling
through `iree-profile`;
- queryable backend statistics for replay, BDA publication, and
timestamp caches;
- stricter unsupported-case handling instead of compatibility-shaped
silent fallback behavior;
- No more C++.

TLDR: the descriptor compatibility path is already materially better
than old Vulkan, the BDA path is the intended fast path and gives Vulkan
native command-buffer replay instead of deferred HAL replay, direct
transfers no longer bounce through emulated command buffers, and the
backend now has the profiling/statistics hooks needed to keep tightening
the hot paths with hard evidence.

Part of #24466 (sub-task: remove deprecated tests under

- `BUILD.bazel` and `CMakeLists.txt` updated to drop matching

- Net diff: 12 files changed, 933 deletions(-), 0 insertions(+)
- No remaining source-tree references to the deleted files
